## Objective

This page makes the simulator-based approximate target explicit on the
augmented parameter-data space. At a fixed positive tolerance, the general
Metropolis–Hastings construction preserves that augmented target. A sequential
population method moves through a declared decreasing sequence of normalized
tolerance targets and corrects its proposal mixtures with Radon–Nikodym
weights. Summary reduction and positive tolerance can bias the target, while
acceptance rates, finite-particle error, and MCMC mixing remain separate
questions.

stated model and does not establish general accuracy or convergence.

## Summary

Approximate Bayesian computation starts with a proper prior, standard-Borel parameter and data spaces, a simulator probability kernel, and a measurable Euclidean summary. For an observed summary $s_0$, the indicator method conditions the prior-simulator law on the closed event $\|S(Y)-s_0\|_2\le\epsilon$. The normalized target is defined only when this event has positive prior-predictive probability; its normalizer is then finite because the joint law is a probability measure. At zero event probability no quotient is assigned.

The rejection procedure repeatedly draws independent prior-simulator pairs and accepts the first pair in the tolerance event. Under its positive-acceptance hypothesis, the local theorem proves almost-sure termination and identifies the accepted parameter law exactly with the tolerance-conditioned target. This exact simulation statement supplies neither a finite-run accuracy guarantee nor an expected proposal-count theorem.

The zero-tolerance result requires a specified jointly measurable summary-density version, almost-everywhere continuity at the observed summary, an integrable envelope on a full closed neighborhood, and finite positive density evidence. Under Countable Choice it proves total-variation convergence to that density-selected summary posterior. It does not select a canonical regular conditional distribution on every marginal-null summary fiber.

A separate sufficient-summary theorem uses a parameter-independent conditional-data kernel under AC to recover a full-data posterior version. Its dominated factorization branch cancels the parameter-independent factor only on the stated finite-positive-evidence fibers. Summary information loss, positive-tolerance bias, and Monte Carlo error therefore remain separate questions. The companion examples include both sufficient and insufficient summaries and a failure of zero-tolerance convergence without the local envelope.

## Summary

These examples isolate the hypotheses behind tolerance-conditioned inference. A proper countable prior with moving summary-density spikes has parameterwise continuity at the observed summary and positive finite density evidence, yet its ABC targets fail to converge to the density-selected update. The local envelope condition cannot be replaced by pointwise continuity alone.

A binary identifiable experiment with a constant summary leaves the ABC target at the prior, demonstrating that full-model identifiability does not establish summary sufficiency. An adjacent-uniform simulator gives an explicit small-tolerance acceptance probability and accepted law, separating exact tolerance-target simulation from the difficulty of obtaining accepted draws.

The finite Bernoulli example works through a sufficient count summary. It computes the full-data and summary likelihood normalizers and verifies a common conditional-data kernel on summary fibers, so the two posterior updates agree in this finite setting. The calculations use the positive-evidence and version conventions of the A page; they claim no generic coverage, contraction, MCMC convergence, or universal acceptance-rate bound.

exact_current_excerpts.excerpt:
## Definition

Use the prior and simulator setup of [[def-approximate-bayesian-computation]]:
standard-Borel parameter and data spaces $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and
$(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, a prior probability $\Pi$, a probability kernel
$K(\theta,\cdot)$, a measurable summary map $S:\mathsf Y\to\mathbb R^d$ with
$d\ge1$, an observed summary $s_0\in\mathbb R^d$, and tolerance
$\epsilon\ge0$. Let
$$B_\epsilon(s_0)=\{s\in\mathbb R^d:\|s-s_0\|_2\le\epsilon\},\qquad A_\epsilon=S^{-1}(B_\epsilon(s_0)).$$
The **prior-simulator joint law** $H$ on the product sigma-algebra
$(\Theta\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y)$ is
$$H(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta),\qquad C_\theta=\{y:(\theta,y)\in C\},$$
which is a probability measure by
[[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. The finite product is standard
Borel by [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]].
Put
$$h_\epsilon(\theta,y)=\mathbf1_{A_\epsilon}(y),\qquad
Z_\epsilon=\int_{\Theta\times\mathsf Y}h_\epsilon\,dH
=\int_\Theta K(\theta,A_\epsilon)\,\Pi(d\theta).$$
Thus $0\le Z_\epsilon\le1$, and $Z_\epsilon$ is the prior-predictive probability
$p_\epsilon(s_0)$ in [[def-approximate-bayesian-computation]]. Only when
$Z_\epsilon>0$ define the **augmented ABC tolerance target**
$$\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon(C)=\frac{1}{Z_\epsilon}\int_C h_\epsilon\,dH
\qquad(C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y).$$
It is the prior-simulator joint law conditioned on the summary-tolerance event.
Its parameter marginal is identified in
[[lem-abc-augmented-target-has-tolerance-posterior-marginal]]. The definition
does not assert that summary reduction or a positive tolerance preserves the
full-data posterior.

## Statement

Under the hypotheses of [[def-abc-augmented-tolerance-target]] with
$Z_\epsilon>0$, the $\Theta$-marginal of
$\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon$ is the tolerance-conditioned law
$\Pi_\epsilon(\cdot\mid s_0)$ defined in
[[def-approximate-bayesian-computation]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A prior probability $\Pi$, simulator probability kernel $K$, measurable
summary $S$, observed summary $s_0$, and $\epsilon\ge0$ with
$Z_\epsilon=p_\epsilon(s_0)>0$.

[F1] [[def-abc-augmented-tolerance-target]]: $H(C)=\int K(\theta,C_\theta)\Pi(d\theta)$,
$A_\epsilon=S^{-1}(B_\epsilon(s_0))$, and
$\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon(C)=Z_\epsilon^{-1}\int_C\mathbf1_{A_\epsilon}(y)\,dH$.

[F2] [[def-approximate-bayesian-computation]]: with $M$ the law of
$(\theta,S(Y))$ under the prior-simulator joint law,
$M(A\times D)=\int_AK(\theta,S^{-1}(D))\Pi(d\theta)$,
$p_\epsilon(s_0)=M(\Theta\times B_\epsilon(s_0))$, and
$\Pi_\epsilon(A\mid s_0)=M(A\times B_\epsilon(s_0))/p_\epsilon(s_0)$.

[F3] [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]: for measurable
$A\subseteq\Theta$ and $D\subseteq\mathsf Y$,
$H(A\times D)=\int_AK(\theta,D)\Pi(d\theta)$.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 For each $A\in\mathcal T$, [F1] and the rectangle formula [F3] give $\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon(A\times\mathsf Y)=Z_\epsilon^{-1}\int_AK(\theta,A_\epsilon)\Pi(d\theta)$. [F1, F3, given]

2.1 Since $A_\epsilon=S^{-1}(B_\epsilon(s_0))$, [F2] gives $M(A\times B_\epsilon(s_0))=\int_AK(\theta,A_\epsilon)\Pi(d\theta)$ and $p_\epsilon(s_0)=Z_\epsilon$; substitution into [F2] makes step 1.1 exactly $\Pi_\epsilon(A\mid s_0)$ for every measurable $A$, so the parameter marginal is the tolerance posterior. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Fix $\epsilon\ge0$ with $Z_\epsilon>0$ and let
$\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon$ be the target in
[[def-abc-augmented-tolerance-target]]. The state is
$x=(\theta,y)\in\Theta\times\mathsf Y$, a standard-Borel product by
[[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]], and
admissible initial states satisfy
$y\in A_\epsilon$. As proposal inputs take a parameter probability kernel
$q(\theta,d\theta')$ and the simulator kernel $K(\theta',dy')$ from
[[def-abc-augmented-tolerance-target]], such that
$$Q((\theta,y),d\theta',dy')=q(\theta,d\theta')K(\theta',dy')$$
is a probability kernel on the augmented state space. Construct the transition
kernel $P_\epsilon$ by applying
[[alg-metropolis-hastings-kernel]] with target
$\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon$ and proposal $Q$. Each iteration proposes a new
parameter from $q$, simulates new data from $K$, applies the general
Metropolis–Hastings accepted-flow rule, and retains the current augmented state
after rejection.

This definition uses one fixed tolerance and the augmented state
$(\theta,y)$. It does not claim irreducibility, uniqueness of a stationary law,
convergence, a mixing rate, or recovery of the full-data posterior.

## Definition

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, $N\ge1$, a positive nonincreasing tolerance
schedule $\epsilon_0\ge\epsilon_1\ge\cdots\ge\epsilon_T>0$, and assume
$Z_{\epsilon_t}>0$ for every $t$. Let
$\widetilde\Pi_{\epsilon_t}$ be the normalized augmented target from
[[def-abc-augmented-tolerance-target]]. The parameter proposal at stage $t$
is a probability kernel $Q_t(\theta,d\theta')$ on $\Theta$.

At stage $0$, draw $(\theta_i,y_i)$ independently from the prior-simulator
law $H$, and set $a_0^i=\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_0}}(y_i)$. If
$\sum_i a_0^i=0$, stop and report finite-particle degeneracy; otherwise
normalize these weights to obtain $W_0^i$.

For each $t=1,\ldots,T$, form the proposal mixture
$$\phi_t^N(\cdot)=\sum_{i=1}^N W_{t-1}^iQ_t(\theta_{t-1}^i,\cdot).$$
Require $\Pi\ll\phi_t^N$.
Here $\Pi\ll\phi_t^N$ means $\phi_t^N(B)=0$ implies $\Pi(B)=0$ for every
$B\in\mathcal T$. Choose a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative
$r_t^N=d\Pi/d\phi_t^N$ supplied by
[[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]]
and [[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
Draw $N$ ancestor indices from the previous weights using the multinomial
branch of [[alg-multinomial-and-residual-offspring-resampling]]. Conditional
on those ancestors, independently draw one perturbed parameter from its
$Q_t$ kernel and one datum from $K$ for each child. For a candidate
$(\theta_t^j,y_t^j)$ set
$$a_t^j=\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_t}}(y_t^j)r_t^N(\theta_t^j).$$
If $\sum_j a_t^j=0$, stop and report finite-particle degeneracy; do not report
a normalized target estimate. If the sum is positive, set
$W_t^j=a_t^j/\sum_k a_t^k$ and report the weighted empirical measure
$\widehat\Pi_t^N=\sum_jW_t^j\delta_{(\theta_t^j,y_t^j)}$.

The mixture support condition is stage-specific and must hold for the actual
previous particle population. The algorithm makes no finite-$N$ accuracy,
mixing, or posterior-recovery claim.

## Statement

Assume AC and the hypotheses of
[[alg-abc-metropolis-hastings]] with $Z_\epsilon>0$. Its output
$P_\epsilon$ is reversible with respect to and leaves invariant the augmented
ABC tolerance target $\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon$ on
$\Theta\times\mathsf Y$. This is invariance for the fixed tolerance target
only; it gives no convergence or full-data posterior conclusion.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a standard-Borel augmented state space, $\epsilon\ge0$ with
$Z_\epsilon>0$, the target $\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon$, the simulator proposal
kernel $Q$, and the ABC-MH procedure.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC states that every family of nonempty sets has
a choice function.

[F1] [[def-abc-augmented-tolerance-target]]: when $Z_\epsilon>0$,
$\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon=Z_\epsilon^{-1}h_\epsilon H$ is a probability measure
on the product of the standard-Borel parameter and data spaces.

[F2] [[alg-abc-metropolis-hastings]]: the algorithm applies
[[alg-metropolis-hastings-kernel]] with target
$\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon$ and proposal probability kernel $Q$, retaining
rejected proposals as self-transitions.

[F3] [[thm-metropolis-hastings-kernel-is-reversible-and-invariant]]: under AC,
for a standard-Borel space, probability target, and probability proposal
kernel, the general Metropolis–Hastings output is reversible with respect to
and leaves invariant its target.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 By [F1], $\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon$ is a probability target on the product state space; by [F2], the proposal is a probability kernel and the returned kernel is exactly the general Metropolis–Hastings output for this target and proposal. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 The state space is standard Borel and [A1] supplies AC, so [F3] applies to the target and proposal identified in step 1.1; it gives reversibility and invariance of $P_\epsilon$ with respect to $\widetilde\Pi_\epsilon$, with no irreducibility or convergence assertion. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the setup of [[alg-abc-sequential-smc]] and put
$$\gamma_t(d\theta,dy)=\Pi(d\theta)K(\theta,dy)\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_t}}(y),
\qquad \pi_t=\gamma_t/Z_{\epsilon_t}=\widetilde\Pi_{\epsilon_t}.$$
For a measure $\mu$, write $\mu(f)=\int f\,d\mu$ for bounded nonnegative
measurable $f$. For every bounded nonnegative product-measurable
$f:\Theta\times\mathsf Y\to[0,\infty)$, let
$X_0^j=(\Theta_0^j,Y_0^j)$, $1\le j\le N$, be the initial $N$ independent
prior-simulator draws with law $H$ and weights
$a_0^j=\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_0}}(Y_0^j)$ satisfy
$$\mathbb E\!\left[\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^Na_0^jf(X_0^j)\right]=\gamma_0(f).$$
For each $1\le t\le T$ and bounded nonnegative product-measurable
$f:\Theta\times\mathsf Y\to[0,\infty)$, condition on a previous weighted particle population
for which $\phi_t^N=\sum_iW_{t-1}^iQ_t(\theta_{t-1}^i,\cdot)$ satisfies
$\Pi\ll\phi_t^N$. Let $r_t^N=d\Pi/d\phi_t^N$ be a finite-valued nonnegative
measurable version, and put
$a_t^j=\mathbf1_{A_{\epsilon_t}}(Y_t^j)r_t^N(\Theta_t^j)$ for the candidates
produced by multinomial ancestor resampling, perturbation, and simulation.
Then
$$\mathbb E\!\left[\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^Na_t^jf(\Theta_t^j,Y_t^j)\,\middle|\,\text{previous population}\right]
=\gamma_t(f).$$
In particular, the average weight is conditionally unbiased for
$Z_{\epsilon_t}$. If candidates with positive total weight are resampled by
the multinomial or residual scheme from normalized weights, then for every
bounded measurable $f$ their conditional empirical mean equals the weighted
candidate empirical mean in expectation. No unbiasedness is asserted for the
self-normalized finite-$N$ estimate, and a finite sample may have zero total
weight or fail to represent positive target mass.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a prior $\Pi$, simulator probability kernel $K$, tolerance event
$A_{\epsilon_t}$, a previous weighted population, mixture $\phi_t^N$,
$\Pi\ll\phi_t^N$, and $Z_{\epsilon_t}>0$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC states that every family of nonempty sets has
a choice function.

[F1] [[def-abc-augmented-tolerance-target]]: the unnormalized augmented target

## Definition

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be standard Borel spaces. Let $\Pi$ be a prior probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and let $K$ be a probability kernel from $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, as in [[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]]. Let $S:\mathsf Y\to\mathbb R^d$ be a measurable statistic for a fixed integer $d\ge1$, and fix an observed summary $s_0\in\mathbb R^d$. The Euclidean norm is $\|x\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d x_j^2)^{1/2}$.

Under the prior-simulator joint law, first draw $\theta\sim\Pi$ and then $Y\sim K(\theta,\cdot)$. The summary-predictive probability measure $M$ on $\Theta\times\mathbb R^d$ is the law of $(\theta,S(Y))$; on measurable rectangles it is
$$M(A\times C)=\int_A K(\theta,S^{-1}(C))\,\Pi(d\theta).$$
The prior and simulator define a joint law by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]], and the change-of-variables formula identifies $M$ as the law after applying $S$ ([[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]).

For $\epsilon\ge0$, define the closed tolerance ball
$$B_\epsilon(s_0)=\{s\in\mathbb R^d:\|s-s_0\|_2\le\epsilon\}.$$
Its prior-predictive acceptance probability is
$$p_\epsilon(s_0):=M(\Theta\times B_\epsilon(s_0))\in[0,1].$$
Only when $p_\epsilon(s_0)>0$ define the indicator ABC target by
$$\Pi_\epsilon(A\mid s_0):=\frac{M(A\times B_\epsilon(s_0))}{p_\epsilon(s_0)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
This is exactly the conditional law of $\theta$ under the augmented event $S(Y)\in B_\epsilon(s_0)$. The denominator is finite because $M$ is a probability, and no quotient is assigned when the event has probability zero. This target is the posterior given a tolerance event, not in general the full-data posterior or the posterior given the exact summary.

## Remarks

A positive tolerance separates summary information loss from tolerance bias; using finitely many accepted draws adds a separate Monte Carlo error. At zero tolerance for an atomless summary the event can have probability zero, so its posterior must be defined through additional density regularity, as in [[thm-abc-zero-tolerance-target-is-summary-posterior-under-density-regularity]].

## Definition

Assume AC. The **Metropolis–Hastings procedure** takes as input a standard-Borel
space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), a target
probability measure $\pi$ ([[def-probability-measure]]), and a probability
kernel $Q$ from $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ to itself
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]).

1. On the product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]),
form the proposal-flow measure $\mu$ ([[def-measure]]) on
$\mathsf X\times\mathsf X$ by
$$\mu(C)=\int_{\mathsf X}Q(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx),\qquad C_x=\{y:(x,y)\in C\}.$$
This is a probability measure by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]].
Let $\tau(x,y)=(y,x)$ and set $\mu^{\mathsf T}(C)=\mu(\tau^{-1}C)$.

2. Set $\eta=\mu\wedge\mu^{\mathsf T}$, the greatest measure dominated by both
flows. Put $\lambda_0=\mu+\mu^{\mathsf T}$, which is a finite measure by
[[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]], and choose nonnegative measurable
representatives $f=d\mu/d\lambda_0$ and $g=d\mu^{\mathsf T}/d\lambda_0$
with $f+g=1$ everywhere after modification on a $\lambda_0$-null set. Define
$$\alpha(x,y)=\begin{cases}\min\{1,g(x,y)/f(x,y)\},&f(x,y)>0,\\1,&f(x,y)=0.\end{cases}$$
This is a jointly measurable version of $d\eta/d\mu$ taking values in $[0,1]$.

3. For $x\in\mathsf X$, compute the integrated acceptance probability
$$a(x)=\int_{\mathsf X}\alpha(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)$$
and rejection probability $r(x)=1-a(x)$.

4. Return the transition rule
$$P(x,A)=\int_{\mathsf X}\mathbf1_A(y)\alpha(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)+\mathbf1_A(x)r(x),\qquad A\in\mathcal X.$$
The second term retains every rejected proposal as a self-transition.

The item [[lem-common-submeasure-and-bounded-radon-nikodym-density]] proves the
common-submeasure construction and density-version claims in step 2.

## Remarks

An RN derivative is an almost-everywhere equivalence class, not a distinguished
pointwise function ([[def-radon-nikodym-derivative]]). The explicit convention
in step 2 selects a measurable version. Changing that version on a $\mu$-null
set leaves the accepted joint flow unchanged, though it can change $P(x,\cdot)$
for a $\pi$-null set of starting states. The theorem
[[thm-metropolis-hastings-kernel-is-reversible-and-invariant]] proves that $P$
is a probability kernel and that $\pi$ is invariant; the procedure alone does
not assert irreducibility, uniqueness, convergence, a rate, or a CLT.

## Statement

Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[alg-metropolis-hastings-kernel]]. Its output
$P$ is a probability kernel, the joint measure
$J_P(dx,dy)=\pi(dx)P(x,dy)$ is symmetric under $(x,y)\mapsto(y,x)$, and $\pi$
is invariant for $P$. Symmetry of this joint measure is reversibility. No
irreducibility, uniqueness, convergence-rate, or central limit theorem
conclusion is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a standard-Borel space, a target probability $\pi$, a proposal
probability kernel $Q$, and the Metropolis–Hastings construction.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC states that every family of nonempty sets has
a choice function.

[F1] [[alg-metropolis-hastings-kernel]]: the algorithm defines
$P(x,A)=\int\mathbf1_A(y)\alpha(x,y)Q(x,dy)+\mathbf1_A(x)r(x)$, where
$\alpha$ is a jointly measurable $[0,1]$-valued version of the accepted-flow
density and $r(x)=1-\int\alpha(x,y)Q(x,dy)$.

[F2] [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]: a probability kernel is a
measurable family of measures with mass one at every source point.

[F3] [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]: for a probability
measure $\pi$ and probability kernel $K$, the formula
$J(C)=\int K(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx)$ defines a probability measure and integrates
nonnegative product-measurable functions by iterated integration.

[F4] [[lem-common-submeasure-and-bounded-radon-nikodym-density]]: the accepted
flow $\eta=\mu\wedge\mu^{\mathsf T}$ is the greatest measure dominated
by both flows, and $\alpha\,\mu=\eta$.

[F5] [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]: integration of a
nonnegative product-measurable function against a probability kernel is a
measurable function of the source point.

[F6] [[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]: $\pi$
is invariant for $P$ when $\int P(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)$ for every measurable
$A$.

[F7] [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: measurable
rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra, so the coordinate-swap map is
measurable.

[F8] [[thm-sections-of-product-measurable-functions-are-measurable]]: each
section of a product-measurable function is measurable.

[F9] [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]: for a
nonnegative measurable $h$, $A\mapsto\int_Ah\,d\nu$ is a measure.

[F10] [[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]]: a finite sum of measures
with nonnegative coefficients is a measure.

[F11] [[def-general-state-reversibility-by-symmetric-flow-measure]]:
reversibility means that the joint flow measure $J_P(dx,dy)=\pi(dx)P(x,dy)$
is symmetric under coordinate swap.

[F12] [[thm-general-state-reversibility-implies-invariance]]: on any measurable
state space, a probability kernel reversible with respect to a probability
measure leaves that measure invariant.

## Proof

**Given:** AC, $\pi$, $Q$, and the procedure in [F1].

1.1 The acceptance function satisfies $0\le\alpha\le1$. For each $x$, $0\le a(x):=\int\alpha(x,y)Q(x,dy)\le1$ because $Q(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure. The function $a$ is measurable by [F5], so $r(x)=1-a(x)$ is measurable and takes values in $[0,1]$. [F1, F5, given]

1.2 Let $J_P$ be the joint measure of $\pi$ and $P$ supplied by [F3]. Splitting its defining integral into accepted and rejected terms gives, for every product measurable $C$, $$J_P(C)=\int\!\int\mathbf1_C(x,y)\alpha(x,y)Q(x,dy)\,\pi(dx) +\int\mathbf1_C(x,x)r(x)\,\pi(dx)=\eta(C)+R(C).$$ The accepted term is $\eta(C)$ by the iterated-integral identity in [F3] for the proposal flow $\mu$ and the density identity $\alpha\,\mu=\eta$ in [F4]. Define $R(C)=\int\mathbf1_C(x,x)r(x)\,\pi(dx)$. [A1, F1, F3, F4, given]

2.1 For fixed $x$, the accepted term $A\mapsto\int\mathbf1_A(y)\alpha(x,y)Q(x,dy)$ is a measure by [F9], since the section $y\mapsto\alpha(x,y)$ is measurable by [F8]. The rejection term $A\mapsto r(x)\mathbf1_A(x)$ is a measure: for disjoint sets at most one can contain $x$. Their sum is a measure by [F10], and its total mass is $a(x)+r(x)=1$. For each fixed $A$, the accepted term is measurable in $x$ by [F5], and the rejection term is measurable since $r$ and $\mathbf1_A$ are measurable. Thus [F2] applies pointwise and $P$ is a probability kernel. [F1, F2, F5, F8, F9, F10, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The coordinate swap $\tau(x,y)=(y,x)$ is measurable by [F7] and is an involution. Since $\eta$ is the greatest measure dominated by both $\mu$ and $\mu^{\mathsf T}$, its transpose $\eta^{\mathsf T}$ is also dominated by both: for every $C$, $\eta^{\mathsf T}(C)=\eta(\tau^{-1}C)\le\mu^{\mathsf T}(C)$ and $\eta^{\mathsf T}(C)\le\mu(C)$. Maximality gives $\eta^{\mathsf T}\le\eta$; transposing this inequality and using $\tau^2=\mathrm{id}$ gives $\eta\le\eta^{\mathsf T}$. Hence $\eta^{\mathsf T}=\eta$. [F4, F7, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 On the diagonal, $\tau(x,x)=(x,x)$, so $\mathbf1_C(x,x)=\mathbf1_{\tau^{-1}C}(x,x)$ for every $x$. Therefore $R(C)=R(\tau^{-1}C)$. Step 2.2 gives the same identity for $\eta$. Combining this with the decomposition in step 1.2 gives $J_P(C)=J_P(\tau^{-1}C)$ for every $C$. Thus the joint flow is symmetric, so $P$ is reversible by [F11]. [F4, F7, F11, step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Steps 2.1 and 3.1 prove that $P$ is a probability kernel reversible with respect to $\pi$. The general-state result [F12] applies on this measurable space and gives $\int P(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal X$. Thus $\pi$ is invariant in the sense of [F6]. [F2, F6, F12, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Definition

Input a particle count $N\ge1$, nonnegative finite weights $a_1,\ldots,a_N$, and a scheme label, either multinomial or residual. Let $A=\sum_{j=1}^Na_j$. If $A>0$, set $p_j=a_j/A$; if $A=0$, set $p_j=1/N$ for every $j$. Thus $p$ is always a probability vector.

- **Multinomial scheme.** Draw an index vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)\in\{1,\ldots,N\}^N$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(J_1=j_1,\ldots,J_N=j_N\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^Np_{j_\ell}$. Put $C_j=\#\{\ell:J_\ell=j\}$.
- **Residual scheme.** Put $q_j=\lfloor Np_j\rfloor$, $r_j=Np_j-q_j$, and $R=\sum_{j=1}^Nr_j=N-\sum_{j=1}^Nq_j$, an integer in $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. If $R=0$, put $C_j=q_j$. If $R>0$, draw $(K_1,\ldots,K_R)$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(K_1=k_1,\ldots,K_R=k_R\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^R(r_{k_\ell}/R)$ and put $C_j=q_j+\#\{\ell:K_\ell=j\}$.

For multinomial resampling, return the sampled vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)$ in its sampled order, together with its count vector $(C_1,\ldots,C_N)$; do not sort the sampled indices. For residual resampling, return the ancestor list containing exactly $C_j$ copies of index $j$, ordered by increasing index, together with its count vector. Each output is a length-$N$ list and a count vector summing to $N$. When all input weights vanish, the uniform fallback defines the procedure; any downstream normalizer already multiplied by this zero average remains zero.

## Remarks

The multinomial branch is the conditionally IID ancestor-index scheme. The residual branch is a distinct selection law: its deterministic floor counts generally make the child indices dependent, while its conditional expected counts agree with the same probability vector.

## Statement

Fix $N\ge1$ and nonnegative input weights $a_1,\ldots,a_N$. Let $p$ be the normalized probability vector, with the uniform fallback when all weights vanish, and let $C_j$ be the offspring count from [[alg-multinomial-and-residual-offspring-resampling]]. Conditional on the input weights, for either scheme and every $1\le j\le N$,
$$\mathbb E[C_j\mid a_1,\ldots,a_N]=Np_j.$$
This assertion concerns the counts only; it gives no variance comparison for arbitrary weights.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite weights, $N\ge1$, and the resampling procedure in the Statement.

[F1] [[alg-multinomial-and-residual-offspring-resampling]]: Multinomial counts are sums of $N$ categorical indicators with probabilities $p_j$; residual counts add $\lfloor Np_j\rfloor$ deterministic copies to categorical draws with probabilities proportional to the fractional remainders.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 In the multinomial branch, $C_j=\sum_{\ell=1}^N\mathbf 1_{\{J_\ell=j\}}$ and each indicator has conditional expectation $p_j$ by the specified product mass. Linearity of a finite sum gives $\mathbb E[C_j\mid a]=Np_j$, including the uniform fallback. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 In the residual branch, write $q_j=\lfloor Np_j\rfloor$ and $r_j=Np_j-q_j$. The remainder $R=\sum_jr_j=N-\sum_jq_j$ is an integer. If $R=0$, every $r_j=0$ and $C_j=q_j=Np_j$; if $R>0$, then $C_j=q_j+\sum_{\ell=1}^{R}\mathbf 1_{\{K_\ell=j\}}$ with each indicator having conditional expectation $r_j/R$, so $\mathbb E[C_j\mid a]=q_j+R(r_j/R)=Np_j$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Steps 1.1 and 1.2 establish the same conditional expected-count identity for both schemes in the procedure, completing the assertion. [step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Remarks

The proof uses only finite sums of categorical indicators and is choice-free. Both schemes satisfy the expected-count interface used by the particle normalizer induction.
